solutions.latex:
In $\triangle BCD$: $\tan 60^\circ=\dfrac{h}{CB}$, so $CB=\dfrac{h}{\tan 60^\circ}=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}$.

In $\triangle ACD$: $\tan 30^\circ=\dfrac{h}{CA}$, so $CA=\dfrac{h}{\tan30^\circ}=\sqrt{3}h$.

Cosine rule in $\triangle ABC$:

$$AB^2=CB^2+CA^2-2(CB)(CA)\cos 60^\circ$$

$$7^2=\left(\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2+\left(\sqrt{3}h\right)^2-2\left(\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\left(\sqrt{3}h\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$$

$$49=\dfrac{h^2}{3}+3h^2-h^2\Rightarrow 147=7h^2\Rightarrow h^2=21$$

Since $h>0$, $h=\sqrt{21}$ metres.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: CB and CA in terms of h; 1: cosine rule substitution; 1: solves h=\sqrt{21}

solutions.latex:
$$A_{\triangle ABC}=\dfrac{1}{2}(CB)(CA)\sin C=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\times\sqrt{3}h\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}h^2=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\times21=\dfrac{21\sqrt{3}}{4}$$

Also $A_{\triangle ABC}=\dfrac{1}{2}\times b\times w$ with $b=7$:

$$\dfrac{21\sqrt{3}}{4}=\dfrac{1}{2}\times7\times w\Rightarrow w=\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}$$

The width of the footpath is $\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}$ metres.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: area using \frac12 ab sin C; 1: equates with \frac12\times7\times w; 1: w=3\sqrt{3}/2

At rest when $v=0$: $-4\cos t=0$, $\cos t=0$, so $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2},\ldots$

$x=\displaystyle\int-4\cos t\,dt=-4\sin t+C$; when $t=0$, $x=1$ so $C=1$, giving $x=1-4\sin t$.

At $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$: $x=-3$.

The particle first comes to rest when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ seconds, 3 m to the left of the origin.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: t = pi/2; 1: x = -3 (3 m to the left of the origin)

solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

$$\text{Distance}=\left|\int_0^{\pi/2}-4\cos t\,dt\right|+\left|\int_{\pi/2}^{2\pi/3}-4\cos t\,dt\right|$$

$$=\left|-4\Big[\sin t\Big]_0^{\pi/2}\right|+\left|-4\Big[\sin t\Big]_{\pi/2}^{2\pi/3}\right|=\left|-4(1-0)\right|+\left|-4\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-1\right)\right|$$

$$=4+4-2\sqrt{3}=8-2\sqrt{3}\text{ metres}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: splits the distance at the change of direction; 1: integrates correctly; 1: total 8 - 2\sqrt{3}

solutions.latex:
Fuel is consumed at $\left(6+\dfrac{v^2}{50}\right)$ L/h and costs $\$0.50$ per litre, so the fuel cost is $\dfrac{1}{2}\left(6+\dfrac{v^2}{50}\right)$ dollars per hour.

Drivers' wages are $\$90$ per hour ($\$45$ each).

$1000$ km at $v$ km/h takes $\dfrac{1000}{v}$ hours.

$$\begin{aligned}C&=\text{fuel}+\text{wages}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(6+\dfrac{v^2}{50}\right)\times\dfrac{1000}{v}+90\left(\dfrac{1000}{v}\right)\\&=\dfrac{500}{v}\left(6+\dfrac{v^2}{50}\right)+\dfrac{90000}{v}\\&=\dfrac{3000}{v}+10v+\dfrac{90000}{v}\\&=10v+\dfrac{93000}{v}\end{aligned}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: cost per hour of fuel and wages and time 1000/v; 1: C = fuel + wages expression; 1: simplifies to 10v + 93000/v

solutions.latex:
$C=10v+93000v^{-1}$, $\dfrac{dC}{dv}=10-\dfrac{93000}{v^2}$.

$\dfrac{dC}{dv}=0$: $93000=10v^2$, $v^2=9300$, $v=\pm\sqrt{9300}$, so $v=10\sqrt{93}\approx96.44$ km/h.

$\dfrac{d^2C}{dv^2}=\dfrac{186000}{v^3}$, which is $>0$ at $v=10\sqrt{93}$, so this is a minimum.

However, at $10\sqrt{93}$ km/h the journey takes $\dfrac{1000}{10\sqrt{93}}\approx10.37$ hours and the speed exceeds the limit of 90 km/h.

For 12 hours, $v=\dfrac{1000}{12}\approx83.33$ km/h. At 90 km/h the journey takes $\dfrac{1000}{90}\approx11.11$ hours, which is within 12 hours.

Since $C$ is decreasing for $v<10\sqrt{93}$, the cost is minimised at the speed limit: $v=90$ km/h.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: differentiates and solves dC/dv = 0; 1: tests minimum and finds v = 10\sqrt{93} approx 96.44; 1: applies the 90 km/h limit and 12 hour constraint, v = 90 km/h
